(p-224) Sūrat al-Aḥzāb

Medinan, and its verses number seventy-three.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O Prophet, fear God.﴾ He addressed him with "the Prophet" and commanded him to be mindful of God (taqwa), out of honour for him and to magnify the matter of taqwa. What is intended is a command to remain steadfast in it, so that it would prevent him from what He forbade in His words: ﴿And do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ in matters that would lead to weakness in the religion.

It is narrated that Abu Sufyan, ʿIkrimah ibn Abi Jahl, and Abu al-Aʿwar al-Sulami came to him concerning the truce (muwada'ah) that existed between him and them, and with them stood Ibn Ubayy, Muʿattib ibn Qushayr, and al-Jadd ibn Qays. They said to him: "Abandon mention of our gods, say that they have intercession, and we will leave you and your Lord alone." So this verse was revealed.

﴿Indeed God is ever Knowing﴾ of the benefits and the harms. ﴿Wise﴾, who judges only in accordance with what wisdom requires.

﴿And follow what is revealed to you from your Lord﴾, as a prohibition against obeying them. ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Acquainted with what you do﴾, so He reveals to you what will make your deeds righteous and will suffice you against listening to the disbelievers. Abu 'Amr read it with the ya' (ي), so that the waw (و) refers to the disbelievers and the hypocrites. That is, Allah is Aware of their schemes and will repel them from you.

﴿And put your trust in Allah﴾: entrust your affair to His management. ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs﴾: the one to whom all affairs are entrusted.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 33, verse 4:**

﴿God has not made for any man two hearts within his body.﴾ That is, He has not joined two hearts in one body, because the heart is the source (*ma'dan*) of the animal spirit (*al-ruh al-hayawani*, the vital spirit) that is first attached to the human soul (*al-nafs al-insaniyya*), and it prevents all the faculties from being shared, and this prevents multiplicity. ﴿Nor has He made your wives whom you divorce by *zihar* (*tuzahirun*) your mothers, nor has He made your adopted sons (*al-di'a*) your sons﴾. He has not combined wifehood and motherhood in one woman, nor calling (adoption) and sonship in one man. The purpose of this is to refute what the Arabs used to claim, that the shrewd and clever man has two hearts; for this reason it was said of Abu Ma'mar, or Jamil ibn Asad al-Fihri, "the one with two hearts." The wife from whom one makes *zihar* is like a mother, and a man's adopted son is his son. For this reason they used to say of Zayd ibn Haritha al-Kalbi, the freedman of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), "the son of Muhammad." Alternatively, the purpose is the negation of motherhood and sonship from the wife one has made *zihar* with and from the adopted son, and the negation of two hearts is a preface to a principle that these two statements rest upon. The meaning is: just as God has not placed two hearts in one body, because that leads to contradiction (namely, that each of them would be the source of all the faculties and not the source of them), He has not made the wife and the adopted son, between whom and him there is no birth relation, into his mother and son, between whom and him there is a birth relation.

Abu 'Amr read *al-lai* with a *ya'* alone, on the basis that its original form is *al-la'* with a *hamza*, which was lightened. The Hijazis read it likewise, and Abu 'Amr, the Hijazis and Ya'qub also read it with the *hamza* alone. The original form of *tuzhirun* is *tatazahharun*, and the second *ta'* was assimilated into the *za'*. Ibn 'Amir read *tazzahirun* with assimilation, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with deletion, and 'Asim read *tuzahirun* from *zahara*. It was also read *tuzhirun* from *zahara* in the sense of *zahara* (to be like), as *'aqada* means *'aqida*, and *tazhurun* from *al-zuhur* (appearing).

The meaning of *zihar* is that a man says to his wife, "You are to me like the back (*zahr*) of my mother," (*kazahri ummi*). It is derived from *al-zahr* (the back) according to the wording, like *talbiya* from *labbayka*. It takes *min* after it because it includes the meaning of abstaining (*al-tajannub*). It was a divorce in the pre-Islamic period, and in Islam it requires either divorce or prohibition until the expiation (*kaffara*) is paid, just as *ala* (to swear not to have intercourse) takes *bi-ha* after it, and it means *halafa* (to swear). The back is mentioned as a euphemism for the belly, of which it is the spine, since mentioning it is close to mentioning the private part; or to intensify the prohibition, for they used to forbid having intercourse with a woman with her back turned toward the sky. *Ad'iya'* is the plural of *da'iyy* in an irregular form, and it seems that it was treated as analogous to *fa'il* in the sense of *fa'il* (agent), so its plural was formed like the plural of that.

﴿That﴾ refers to what has been mentioned, or to the last of them. ﴿Your saying with your mouths﴾ has no reality in external existence, like the words of one who raves. ﴿But God says the truth﴾, which has an external reality corresponding to it. ﴿And He guides to the way﴾, the way of truth.

﴿Call them by their fathers' names﴾: attribute them to their fathers (انْسِبُوهم). This singles out the intended meaning from among his true statements. His saying ﴿That is more just in the sight of God﴾ gives the reason for it. The pronoun refers to the verbal noun of (ادْعُوهم, "call them"). (أقْسَطُ, "more just") is an elative used to denote excess in an absolute sense, derived from qist, meaning justice, and its meaning is the one that reaches the utmost in truthfulness. ﴿And if you do not know their fathers﴾ so that you can attribute them to them, ﴿then they are your brothers in religion﴾, that is, they are your brothers in religion, ﴿and your clients﴾, that is, your allies in it. So say, "This is my brother and my client," with this interpretation. ﴿And there is no blame upon you for what you have erred in﴾: there is no sin upon you for what you did of that kind while mistaken, either before the prohibition or after it, through forgetfulness or a slip of the tongue. ﴿But what your hearts have intended﴾: rather, the blame lies in what your hearts have intended, or, alternatively, the blame lies in what your hearts have intended concerning it. ﴿And God is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾, for His pardon of the one who errs.

Know that adoption (tabanni) has no legal effect according to us, while according to Abu Hanifa it requires the freeing of the adopter's slave and establishes lineage for an unknown person to whom it is possible to attach him.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 33, verse 6:

﴿The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves﴾ in all matters, for he does not command them, nor is he pleased with them, except with what is good for them and their success, unlike the self, which is why he is absolute. It is therefore obligatory upon them that he be more beloved to them than their own selves, that his command be more binding upon them than the command of their selves, and that their affection for him be more complete than their affection for themselves.

It is narrated: "When he, upon him be prayers and peace, intended the expedition to Tabuk, he commanded the people to set out. Some people said: 'We will ask permission from our fathers and our mothers,' so this was revealed."

It was also read "and he is a father to them" (wa-huwa abun lahum), i.e. in religion, for every prophet is a father to his community in that he is the source of that by which eternal life is attained; and for this reason the believers became brothers. ﴿And his wives are their mothers﴾, placed in the station of mothers in prohibition (of marriage) and in deserving veneration; and in other respects they are like non-related women. For this reason 'Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "We are not the mothers of women." ﴿And those of blood-relationship﴾, i.e. those who are related by kinship. ﴿Are closer to one another﴾ in inheritance, and this abrogates what was in early Islam concerning inheritance by emigration and by allegiance in religion. ﴿In the Book of Allah﴾, i.e. in the Preserved Tablet, or in what was revealed, which is this verse, or the verse of inheritance, or in what Allah has enjoined. ﴿Of the believers and the emigrants﴾ is an explanation of "those of blood-relationship," or it is a complement to "closer" — i.e., those of blood-relationship, by the right of kinship, are closer in inheritance than the believers by the right of religion and than the emigrants by the right of emigration. ﴿Except that you do a kindness to your allies﴾ is an exception from the most general category of benefit in which closeness is to be understood; and the intended meaning of doing a kindness is bequest, or it is a disjunctive exception. ﴿That was in the Book inscribed﴾: what was mentioned in the two verses was established in the Tablet or the Qur'an. It is also said: in the Torah.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 33, verse 7–8:

﴿And [remember] when We took from the Prophets their covenant﴾ is governed by an implied "remember" (udhkur). Their covenant (mithaq) refers to their pledges to convey the message and to call to the upright religion.

﴿And from you, and from Noah, and Abraham, and Moses, and Jesus, son of Mary﴾ He specified them for mention because they are the famous possessors of revealed laws (arbab al-shara'i'). He placed our Prophet (ﷺ) first, honouring him and exalting his station.

﴿And We took from them a solemn covenant﴾ great in importance, or confirmed by oath. The repetition serves to explain this attribute, magnifying it.

﴿That He may question the truthful about their truthfulness﴾ That is, We did this so that God, on the Day of Resurrection, might question the Prophets who were true to their covenant about what they conveyed to their peoples; or [it means] their confirmation of them, as a rebuke; or [it means] the believers who confirmed them, about their confirmation, for the confirmer of the truthful is himself truthful; or [it means] the believers who were true to their covenant when He made them witness against themselves, about their truthfulness in their covenant. ﴿And He has prepared for the disbelievers a painful punishment﴾ This is conjoined to ("We took") from the standpoint that the sending of the messengers and the taking of the covenant from them were for the reward of the believers; or it is conjoined to what is indicated by "that He may question" – as if he said: "So He rewarded the believers and prepared for the disbelievers."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 33, verse 9:

﴿O you who believe, remember the favour of Allah upon you when hosts came against you﴾. He means the confederates (al-Ahzab), who were the Quraysh, Ghatafan, and the Jews of Banu Qurayzah and al-Nadir, and they were about twelve thousand in number. ﴿Then We sent against them a wind﴾, namely the east wind (rih al-Saba). ﴿And hosts you did not see﴾, namely the angels.

It is narrated that when the Prophet (ﷺ) heard of their approach, he dug the trench (al-khandaq) around Madinah, then went out to meet them with three thousand men, with the trench between him and them. About a month passed over the two parties with no fighting between them except exchanging arrows and stones, until Allah sent upon them a cold wind on a wintry night. It chilled them severely, blew dust into their faces, extinguished their fires, uprooted their tents, and the horses surged against one another, while the angels shouted takbir on the sides of the army. Then Talihah ibn Khuwaylid al-Asadi said, "As for Muhammad, he has already begun you with sorcery, so save yourselves, save yourselves!" And they fled without any fighting.

﴿And Allah is ever, of what you do﴾, namely of digging the trench. Al-Basriyyan read it with the yaa (ya'malun), meaning of what the polytheists do of confederating and warring. ﴿Seeing﴾, i.e., ever-seeing.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 33, verse 10:

﴿When they came upon you﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿when there came upon you﴾. ﴿From above you﴾: from the upper part of the valley, from the direction of the east, were the Banu Ghatafan. ﴿And from below you﴾: from the lower part of the valley, from the direction of the west, were the Quraysh. ﴿And when the eyes swerved﴾: they turned away from the level of their gaze, out of bewilderment and staring fixedly. ﴿And the hearts reached the throats﴾: from terror, for the lung swells from the intensity of fright, so the heart rises with its rise up to the top of the throat (hanjarah), which is the end of the windpipe (hulqum), the passage of food and drink. ﴿And you assumed about God assumptions﴾: various kinds of assumption. So the sincere ones, firm of heart, assumed that God would fulfil His promise of raising His religion, or that He was testing them, so they feared slipping and weakness of endurance; and the weak of heart and the hypocrites assumed what has been related of them. The alif in such words is added (mazidah) as a assimilation of the fawasil (verse endings) to the qawafi (rhyme endings). Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr applied the wasl (connection) to it as the waqf (pause), while Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and Ya'qub did not add it in an absolute sense, and this is the analogical rule (al-qiyas).

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on Surah 33, verses 11–12:**

﴿There the believers were tested﴾: they were examined, so the sincere was distinguished from the hypocrite, and the steadfast from the wavering. ﴿And they were shaken with a severe shaking﴾ from the intensity of the terror. It is also recited (*qira'a*, a recitation variant) as «زَلْزالًا» with a fatha.

﴿And when the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease said﴾: weakness of belief. ﴿"What Allah and His Messenger promised us"﴾: of victory and the elevation of the religion. ﴿"was nothing but delusion"﴾: a false promise. It was said that the one who spoke this was Mu'attib ibn Qushayr, who said: "Muhammad promises us the conquest of Persia and Rome, while one of us cannot even relieve himself out of fear. This is nothing but a promise of delusion."(p-227)

This is nothing but a promise of delusion."(p-227)

And when a group of them said, "O people of Yathrib (Medina)! There is no place for you to stand, so turn back." [This refers to Aws ibn Qayzi and his followers.] "O people of Yathrib" means the people of Medina; it is also said that Yathrib is the name of a land of which Medina lies in one part.

"No place to stand" means no station of standing. "For you" here; Hafs read it with a ḍammah (muqām), on the basis that it is a place or a verbal noun from aqāma (to stay).

"So turn back" means return to your dwellings fleeing. It is also said that the meaning is: there is no place for you to stand on the religion of Muhammad, so return to polytheism and submit to it so that you may be safe; or: there is no place for you to stay in Yathrib, so return as disbelievers so that you may be able to remain there.

"And a party of them asks leave of the Prophet" to return. "They say, 'Our houses are exposed'" — unprotected and not secure; its root meaning is a defect (khalal). It is permissible that the word ʿawrah be derived from "ʿawirat al-dār," when the house becomes defective; and it has been read with this sense.

"And they are not exposed" — rather, they are secure. "They only intend to flee" — that is, they do not intend by this except to flee from fighting.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 33, verse 14:

﴿And if it had been entered upon them﴾ — the city, or their houses, had been entered "from its sides" — ﴿from its surrounding areas﴾, i.e., from its sides. The agent (the one doing the entering) is omitted to indicate that the entry of these factious allies (al-Mutahazzibin) upon them and the entry of other armies are equal in necessitating the ruling that follows from it. ﴿Then they were asked for sedition﴾ — that is, apostasy (riddah) and fighting the Muslims. ﴿They would have given it⁠﴾ — i.e., they would have granted it (la-atawha, from ataw, "to give"). The two Hijazi readers (Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr) read it with the short vowel (la-ataha/"la-jaaha" form in the sense of "they would have come to it and done it" — lajaʾū-hā wa-fa'alūhā). ﴿And they would not have delayed in it⁠﴾ — i.e., in the sedition or in granting it. ﴿Except briefly⁠﴾ — just for the time it takes for the question and the answer to occur. It has also been said: they would not have remained in Medina after the completion of the apostasy except briefly.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 33, verses 15–16:

﴿And indeed they had already made a covenant with Allah before, that they would not turn their backs.﴾ He means the Banu Harithah, who made a covenant with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the day of Uhud, when they lost their resolve (fashilu), and then repented that they would not return to the like of it. ﴿And the covenant of Allah will be questioned﴾ concerning fulfilling it; he will be requited for it.

﴿Say: Flight will not benefit you if you flee from death or killing.﴾ For every person must die by a natural death (hatf anf), or by being killed at a specific time that has been decreed beforehand and that the Pen has written. ﴿And then you will not be given enjoyment except for a little﴾ — that is, even if flight were to benefit you, for example, by granting you enjoyment through delay, that enjoyment would be nothing but a small enjoyment, or a short period of time.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 33, verses 17–18:

﴿Say, "Who is it that can protect you from Allah if He intends for you harm, or intends for you mercy?"﴾ That is: or He will afflict you with harm if He intends mercy for you. He has abbreviated the speech, as in his saying:

*"Wearing a sword and a spear"*

Or the second is taken as governed by the first, because the notion of prevention (man') is inherent in "protection" (ʿişma). ﴿And they will not find for themselves any ally other than Allah﴾ who would benefit them. ﴿Nor any helper﴾ who would repel harm from them.

﴿Allah already knows those among you who hinder (al-muʿawwiqin)﴾ those who discourage (al-muthabbitin) people from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they are the hypocrites. ﴿And those who say to their brothers﴾ among the inhabitants of Madinah: ﴿"Come here to us"﴾ that is, bring yourselves close to us. Its root has been mentioned in al-Anʿam. ﴿And they do not come to the fight except a little﴾ except a coming, or a time, or a little fighting. For they make excuses and discourage (others) as much as they can, or they go out with the believers but do not fight except a little, like His saying ﴿They did not fight except a little﴾. It has also been said that this is part of their own speech, and its meaning is: the companions of Muhammad will not come to the battle of the Confederates (al-Ahzab), nor will they confront them except a little.

﴿Stingy towards you﴾: withholding from you assistance, or spending in the way of God, or victory, or booty. It is the plural of *shaḥīḥ* (شَحِيحٍ), and its accusative form is either a *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative, a state of the subject) from the subject of *yaʾtūna* (يَأْتُونَ) or *al-muʿawwiqīn* (المُعَوِّقِينَ), or an accusative of *dhamm* (vituperation, censure). ﴿So when fear comes, you see them looking at you, their eyes rolling﴾ in their sockets. ﴿Like one who faints from death﴾: like the gaze of one who has fainted, or like the rolling of his eyes, or they are compared to such a person, or the comparison is to his very eye. ﴿From death﴾: from the agony of death's pangs, out of fear and clinging to you. ﴿When fear departs﴾ and the spoils have been secured. ﴿They will lash you﴾: they will strike you ﴿with sharp tongues﴾, pointed ones, seeking booty. *Salq* (السَّلْقُ) means spreading out forcefully, by hand or by tongue.

﴿Stingy towards good﴾: it is in the accusative as a *ḥāl* or as *dhamm*. The reading in the nominative (*rafʿ*) supports this, and it is not a repetition, because each of the two is restricted in some respect. ﴿Those have not believed﴾ sincerely. ﴿So God has nullified their deeds﴾: He made their invalidity manifest, since no deeds of theirs were established so as to be nullified; or He nullified their pretence and hypocrisy. ﴿And that﴾ nullification ﴿is for God easy﴾: effortless, because His will is attached to it and nothing prevents Him from it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 33, verse 20:

﴿They think the confederates have not withdrawn﴾ That is, these people, out of their cowardice, suppose that the confederates have not been routed, when in fact they have been routed and have fled into the interior of Medina. ﴿And if the confederates should come again﴾ in a second assault. ﴿They would wish that they were in the desert among the Bedouins﴾ they would wish they were outside in the wilderness, living among the Bedouin Arabs. ﴿Asking about your news﴾ asking every arrival from the direction of Medina ﴿about your news﴾ about what has befallen you.

﴿And even if they had been among you﴾ during this assault, and had not returned to Medina, and there had been fighting, ﴿they would not have fought except a little﴾ for show, and out of fear of reproach.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 33, verse 21:**

﴿Indeed, in the Messenger of God you have a good example﴾: a good quality which deserves to be emulated, such as steadfastness in war and endurance of hardships. Or it means that he himself is an exemplar worthy of emulation, like your saying, "In the egg there are twenty *mann* of iron" (*mann*, a unit of weight), meaning that the egg itself contains this amount of iron. ʿĀṣim read *uswah* with a *ḍammah* on the *hamzah* (*ʾuswah*), and this is a dialectal variant of the word (*lughah*).

﴿For whoever hopes for God and the Last Day﴾: that is, hopes for the reward of God or for meeting Him and the bliss of the Hereafter, or, specifically, for the days of God (*ayyām Allah*) and the Last Day. It has also been said that it is like your saying, "I hope for Zayd and his bounty," since the Last Day is included within that hope in terms of its ruling. *Al-rajāʾ* (hope) may include both hope and fear. The clause *li-man kāna* (for whoever was) is either a *ṣilah* (relative clause) for *ḥasanah* (good) or a *ṣifah* (qualifier) for it. It has also been said that it is a *badal* (substitute, in apposition) for *lakum* (for you), but most grammarians hold that a pronoun of address cannot be replaced in this way.

﴿And remembers God much﴾: He combined hope with frequent remembrance of God, which leads to constant obedience, since whoever emulates the Messenger is one who is like this.

"When the believers saw the confederates, they said, 'This is what Allah and His Messenger promised us,' in accordance with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or do you think that you will enter Paradise while there has not yet come to you the example of those who passed away before you?﴾ — the verse — and His saying, peace and blessings be upon him: 'The matter will become severe with the confederates gathering against you, but the final outcome will be yours over them.' And His saying, peace and blessings be upon him: 'Verily, they will march against you after nine or ten [nights].' Hamzah and Abu Bakr read [the verb] with a kasra on the ra' and a fatha on the hamza [i.e., as 'ara' ... with the verb form read as 'ra'a' in the active-passive sense, adjusting the vowels accordingly]. ﴿And Allah and His Messenger spoke truly﴾: the truthfulness of the report of Allah and His Messenger became manifest, or they were truthful in the help and the reward just as they were truthful in the trial. The placing of the Name (Allah) here is for glorification. ﴿And it increased them not﴾: the pronoun in it refers to the [subject of] "when they saw" (ra'aw), or to the matter (al-khatb), or to the trial (al-bala'). ﴿except in faith﴾ in Allah and His promises. ﴿and submission﴾ to His commands and His decrees."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 33, verses 23–24:

﴿Among the believers are men who have been true to what they covenanted with God﴾: that is, in steadfastness with the Messenger (ﷺ) and in fighting to raise the religion. It is from *ṣadaqanī* (he spoke the truth to me) when he says to you the truth: for one who is bound by a covenant, when he fulfils his covenant, he has been true in it. ﴿Among them is one who has fulfilled his vow﴾: his *nadhr* (vow), by fighting until he was martyred, like Ḥamzah, Muṣ'ab ibn 'Umayr and Anas ibn al-Naḍr. *Al-naḥb* means the vow, and it was borrowed for death, because it is like an obligatory vow upon the neck of every living being. ﴿And among them is one who awaits﴾ martyrdom, like 'Uthmān and Ṭalḥah, may God be pleased with them both. ﴿And they did not change﴾ the covenant, nor altered it. ﴿Not in the least alteration﴾: they did not change it in any degree of alteration.

It was narrated that "Ṭalḥah remained with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on the day of Uḥud until his hand was struck, and the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: 'Ṭalḥah has made it obligatory [for himself]'." In this there is an allusion to the people of hypocrisy and sickness of the heart who changed their position. His saying:

﴿So that God may reward the truthful for their truthfulness and punish the hypocrites if He wills, or turn to them in forgiveness﴾ is a statement of cause for what was expressed explicitly and what was alluded to. It is as if the hypocrites intended by the change the evil outcome, just as the sincere ones intended by steadfastness and fidelity the good outcome. Turning to them in mercy is conditional upon their repentance, or what is meant by it is granting them success in repenting. ﴿Indeed God is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾ toward whoever repents.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 33, verse 25:

﴿And Allah turned back those who disbelieved﴾ meaning the confederates (al-Ahzab). ﴿In their rage﴾, being enraged. ﴿They gained no good﴾ being not victorious. These two are circumstantial clauses (hal), either by overlap (tadakhul) or by succession (ta'aqub). ﴿And Allah sufficed the believers in the fighting﴾ by means of the wind and the angels. ﴿And Allah is ever Strong﴾ over bringing about whatever He wills. ﴿Mighty﴾, prevailing over everything.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 33, verse 26:

﴿And He brought down those of the People of the Book who supported them﴾ who supported the confederates (al-aḥzāb). ﴿from their strongholds﴾ from their fortresses. The singular is ṣayṣiyah (a stronghold), which is that by which one fortifies oneself. For this reason the horn of a bull or a gazelle and the spur of a rooster are called ṣayṣiyah. ﴿And He cast terror into their hearts﴾ fear. It is also read with a ḍammah on the first letter (ar-ruʿb). ﴿Some you killed, and some you took captive﴾ It is also read with a ḍammah on the sīn (the first letter of the verb). It was reported: "Jibril came to the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, on the morning of the night in which the confederates were routed, and said: 'Have you laid down your weapons? The angels have not laid down their weapons. God commands you to march against the Banu Qurayzah, and I am heading toward them.' So he proclaimed among the people that no one should pray the ʿaṣr prayer except in the land of the Banu Qurayzah. He besieged them for twenty-one or twenty-five days until the siege bore heavily upon them. He said to them, 'Come down under my judgment,' but they refused. He said, 'Then under the judgment of Saʿd ibn Muʿadh,' and they agreed to it. Saʿd ruled that their fighting men be killed, and their children and women taken captive. The Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, exclaimed Allahu akbar, and said, 'You have judged by the judgment of God from above the seven heavens.'" So they killed six hundred or more of them, and took seven hundred captive.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 33, verse 27:

﴿And He caused you to inherit their land﴾ (i.e., their fields, مَزارِعَهم). ﴿and their homes﴾ (i.e., their fortresses, حُصُونَهم). ﴿and their wealth﴾ (i.e., their money, livestock, and goods, نُقُودَهم ومَواشِيَهم وأثاثَهم).

It is narrated that "the Prophet (ﷺ) made their estates (عَقارَهم) for the Muhajirun, and the Ansar spoke about this. So he said: 'You have your dwellings.' And 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: 'Will you not take a fifth of it as you took a fifth on the day of Badr?' He said: 'No, these were given to me only as a special provision (طُعْمَةً).'"

﴿And a land you had not trodden﴾: like Persia and Rome. It is said it refers to Khaybar, and it is said it refers to every land that will be conquered until the Day of Resurrection. ﴿And Allah is ever over all things competent﴾: so He is able to do that.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 33, verse 28–29:

﴿O Prophet, say to your wives: If you desire the life of this world and its adornment,﴾ the abundance and luxury therein. ﴿And its adornment﴾ its ornaments.

﴿Then come, I will provide for you (umatti'kunna)﴾ I will give you a provision (al-mut'ah). ﴿And release you in a fair release﴾ divorce without harm and without innovation (bid'ah).

It is narrated that they asked him for garments of adornment and an increase in maintenance, so this was revealed. He began with ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, and offered her the choice, and she chose Allah and His Messenger. Then the rest of the wives chose as she had chosen, so Allah thanked them for that, and He revealed ﴿Women are not lawful to you after this﴾. The making of the release conditional upon their desire for the worldly life, and placing it as the counterpart of their desire for the Messenger, indicates that the one given the choice, if she chooses her husband, is not divorced. This is contrary to Zayd, al-Hasan, Malik, and one of the two narrations from ʿAlī. It is supported by the statement of ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave us the choice, and we chose him," and she did not count it as a divorce. The placing of the provision (al-tamattuʿ) before the release that is caused by it reflects generosity and good character. It is said that this is because the separation was by their own will, like the choice of the one given the choice herself, for it is a revocable divorce according to us and an irrevocable one according to the Ḥanafiyyah. There is disagreement over whether it is obligatory for the one who has been consummated with, and there is nothing in it that indicates that.

It was also read as "umatti'kunna wa-usarriḥkunna" with the raf' (nominative), as a resumptive construction (al-istiʾnaf).

﴿And if you desire Allah and His Messenger and the Last Abode, then indeed Allah has prepared for the good-doers among you a great reward﴾ the world and its adornment are belittled in comparison to it. The word "min" (among) here is explicative (lil-tabyin), because all of them were good-doers.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 33, verses 30–31:

﴿O wives of the Prophet, whoever of you commits a clear indecency﴾ (fahisha), a grave sin. ﴿Mubayyina﴾, meaning its ugliness is manifest, according to the recitation of Ibn Kathir and Abu Bakr, while the rest read it with a kasra under the ya'. ﴿Her punishment will be doubled twofold﴾, meaning twice the punishment of other women, i.e. double it, because the sin from them is more heinous, since the increase in its ugliness follows the increase in the excellence of the sinner and in the blessing bestowed upon them. For this reason the prescribed punishment for a free woman was made twice that of a slave, and the Prophets were admonished with what others are not admonished for. Al-Basriyyan read ﴿yudaaf﴾ (yuḍā‘af, passive voice) with ﴿al-adhab﴾ (the punishment) in the nominative. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Amir read ﴿nudaaf﴾ with the nun and the active voice, with ﴿al-adhaba﴾ (the punishment) in the accusative. ﴿And that is ever easy for Allah﴾: the fact that they are the wives of the Prophet does not prevent Him from doubling it, and how could it, when He is its cause?

﴿And whoever of you is devoutly obedient﴾ (yaqnut), that is, whoever persists in obedience. ﴿To Allah and His Messenger﴾. Perhaps the mention of Allah here is for magnification, or it is for His saying: ﴿and does righteous deeds, We shall give her her reward twice﴾, once for the obedience and once for seeking the pleasure of the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, through contentment and good companionship. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿wa-yaʿmal﴾ with the ya', treating it as agreeing with the wording of ﴿man﴾ (whoever) and ﴿wa-yu'tiha﴾, on the basis that within it is a pronoun referring to the name of Allah. ﴿And We have prepared for her a noble provision﴾ in Paradise, in addition to her reward.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 33, verses 30–31:

﴿O wives of the Prophet, whoever of you commits a clear indecency﴾ (fahisha), a grave sin. ﴿Mubayyina﴾, meaning its ugliness is manifest, according to the recitation of Ibn Kathir and Abu Bakr, while the rest read it with a kasra under the ya'. ﴿Her punishment will be doubled twofold﴾, meaning twice the punishment of other women, i.e. double it, because the sin from them is more heinous, since the increase in its ugliness follows the increase in the excellence of the sinner and in the blessing bestowed upon them. Perhaps the mention of Allah here is for magnification, or it is for His saying: ﴿and does righteous deeds, We shall give her her reward twice﴾, once for the obedience and once for seeking the pleasure of the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, through contentment and good companionship. ﴿O wives of the Prophet, you are not like any of the women﴾. The origin of *aḥad* (أحد) is *waḥd*, meaning "one" (*al-wāḥid*). It was then used in a general negation, where it applies equally to the masculine and feminine, and to the singular and plural. The meaning is: you are not like one group among the groups of women in excellence (*faḍl*). ﴿If you fear God﴾, meaning, if you oppose the command of God and the pleasure of His Messenger. ﴿then do not be soft in speech﴾, meaning, do not speak in a yielding, gentle tone like the speech of women who arouse suspicion (*al-murībāt*). ﴿lest he in whose heart is a disease should covet﴾, meaning, lest there be immorality (*fujūr*). It is also read with the jussive *fayaṭma'a* (فَيَطْمَعَ), as a conjunction on the place of the prohibitive verb (*fi'l al-nahy*, the verb of prohibition, here the form after *lā*), on the basis that the one with a diseased heart was forbidden from coveting immediately after their being forbidden to speak in a yielding tone. ﴿And speak a known word﴾, meaning, a good word, far from anything that raises suspicion.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 33, verse 33:

﴿And remain in your houses﴾ from waqara, yaqiru, waqaran, or from qarra, yaqarru. The first of the two identical letters (rā’) of iqrarna (“remain”) was deleted and its kasra was transferred to the qāf, so that the hamzat al-wasl (the connecting hamza) was dispensed with. This is supported by the reading of Nafi‘ and ‘Asim with a fatha, from qarartu, aqarru, which is a dialect form of it. It is also possible that it derives from qara, yaqarru, meaning “to gather.” ﴿And do not display yourselves⌋ ﴾ — wa la tabarrajna — meaning do not strut and sway in your walking. ﴿The display of the former ignorance﴾ — tabarruj-an mithla tabarruj al-nisa’ fi ayyam al-jahiliyyah al-qadimah (a display like the display of women in the days of the ancient jahiliyyah, the pre-Islamic age of ignorance). It has also been said that it refers to the period between Adam and Noah. It has also been said that it refers to the time in which Abraham, peace be upon him, was born, when women would wear a garment of pearls and walk in the middle of the road, displaying themselves to men. The “other jahiliyyah” is the period between Jesus and Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon them both. It has also been said that the “former jahiliyyah” is the jahiliyyah of disbelief before Islam, and the “other jahiliyyah” is the jahiliyyah of wickedness within Islam. This is strengthened by his saying, peace be upon him, to Abu al-Darda’, may Allah be pleased with him: “Indeed, there is jahiliyyah in you.” He said: “Is it jahiliyyah of disbelief or of Islam?” He said: “Rather, it is jahiliyyah of disbelief.”

﴿And establish the prayer, and give the zakat, and obey Allah and His Messenger﴾ in all that He has commanded you and forbidden you. ﴿Indeed, Allah intends only to remove from you the defilement﴾ — al-dhanb al-mudannis li-‘irdikum (the sin that soils your honour). This is a justification for their commands and prohibitions, stated as a new sentence (istinaf), and for this reason the ruling was generalised. ﴿O people of the household﴾ — nusiba ‘ala al-nida’ aw al-madh (it is in the accusative either as a vocative or as a term of praise).

﴿And purify you﴾ from acts of disobedience. ﴿with thorough purification﴾. The use of “defilement” as a metaphor for disobedience, and the completion of the metaphor with “purification,” serve to repel one from it. The Shi‘ah restrict “the people of the household” to Fatimah, ‘Ali, and their two sons, may Allah be pleased with them, on the basis of what is reported: that he, peace be upon him, went out one morning wearing a striped cloak of black wool. Fatimah, may Allah be pleased with her, came, and he admitted her into it; then ‘Ali came, and he admitted him into it; then al-Hasan and al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them both, came, and he admitted them into it; then he said: ﴿Indeed, Allah intends only to remove from you the defilement, O people of the household﴾. Yet the argument from this for their infallibility (‘ismah) and for the binding force of their consensus (ijma‘) as proof is weak, because restricting it to them does not fit what precedes and follows the verse, and the hadith implies that they are among the people of the household, not that no one else is.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 33, verse 34:

﴿And remember what is recited in your houses of the signs of Allah and the wisdom.﴾ That is, of the Book, which combines both matters (i.e., the signs and the wisdom). It is a reminder of the favour Allah has bestowed upon them, in that He made them the people of the House of Prophethood (ahl bayt al-nubuwwah) and the place of descent of revelation (mahbit al-wahy), and of what they witnessed of the hardship of revelation (bura'a al-wahy), which necessarily produces strength of faith and eagerness for obedience, as an incitement to refrain (from what is forbidden) and to comply (with what they have been charged with). ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Subtle, Acquainted.﴾ He knows and arranges what is suitable in the religion; therefore He gave you the choice (khayyara) and admonished you. Or (it means): He knows who is fit for His prophethood and who is fit to be its people (ahl baytih).(p-232)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 33, verse 35:

﴿Indeed, the Muslim men and Muslim women﴾ those who have entered into submission (al-silm) and who submit to the command of Allah. ﴿And the believing men and believing women﴾ those who affirm what they must affirm. ﴿And the obedient men and obedient women﴾ those who persist in obedience. ﴿And the truthful men and truthful women﴾ in speech and deed. ﴿And the patient men and patient women﴾ in acts of obedience and in refraining from sins. ﴿And the humble men and humble women﴾ those who are humbled before Allah with their hearts and their limbs. ﴿And the charitable men and charitable women﴾ those who give what is obligatory from their wealth. ﴿And the fasting men and fasting women﴾ those who observe the obligatory fast. ﴿And the men who guard their private parts and the women who guard them﴾ from what is unlawful. ﴿And the men who remember Allah much and the women who remember Him﴾ with their hearts and their tongues. ﴿Allah has prepared for them forgiveness﴾ for the minor sins they have committed, because these (acts) are expiating. ﴿And a great reward﴾ for their obedience. The verse is a promise to them and to those like them for obedience and for adorning themselves (al-tadarru') with these qualities.

It is narrated: "That the wives of the Prophet ﷺ said: 'O Messenger of Allah, Allah has mentioned the men in the Qur'an with goodness, but there is no good among us by which we are mentioned,' and so this was revealed."

It is also said: when what was revealed concerning them was revealed, the women of the Muslims said, "Nothing has been revealed concerning us," and so this was revealed.

The conjunction of the females with the males is because the two sexes differ, and it is necessary (daruri). The conjunction of the spouses with the spouses (i.e., the pairs of qualities) is because the two descriptions differ, so it is not necessary; for this reason it was omitted in His saying (﴿Muslimat, mu'minat﴾). Its benefit is to indicate that the preparation of forgiveness and reward is for those who combine these qualities.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 33, verse 36:

﴿It is not for a believing man or a believing woman﴾ — it is not proper for him. ﴿When Allah and His Messenger have decreed a matter﴾ — that is, when the Messenger of Allah has decreed. Allah is mentioned to magnify his command and to indicate that his decree is the decree of Allah. It was revealed concerning Zaynab bint Jahsh, the daughter of his paternal aunt Umaymah bint Abd al-Muttalib, whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) proposed for marriage to Zayd ibn Harithah, but she and her brother Abd Allah refused. It is also said that it concerned Umm Kulthum bint Uqbah, who had given herself to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he married her to Zayd. ﴿They should have no choice in their affair﴾ — that they should not choose anything of their affair; rather, it is obligatory upon them to make their choice follow the choice of Allah and His Messenger. Al-khiyarah (choice) is that which is chosen. The pronoun of the first (plural) is in the plural because of the generality of "believing man or believing woman," since they both occur in a context of negation, while the plural of the second (pronoun) is for magnification. The Kufans and Hisham read «yakūna» with the ya' (yā’). ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger has certainly strayed into clear error﴾ — he has clearly deviated from the right course.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 33, verse 37:

﴿And when you said to him on whom Allah had bestowed favour﴾ by His enabling him to accept Islam, and your enabling him to be freed (*'itq*, manumission) and singled out for closeness, ﴿and you had bestowed favour upon him﴾ by what Allah had enabled you to do regarding him, and he was Zayd ibn Harithah, ﴿"Keep your wife to yourself"﴾ Zaynab. The reason was that: "He, upon whom be blessings and peace, saw her after he had married her to him, and she came into his heart, so he said, 'Glory be to Allah, the Turner of hearts.' Zaynab heard the glorification and mentioned it to Zayd, and he perceived this, and the aversion to her companionship entered his heart. So he came to the Prophet, upon whom be blessings and peace, and said, 'I want to separate from my companion.' He said, 'What is the matter with you? Has anything from her made you doubt?' He said, 'No, by Allah, I have seen from her nothing but good, but because of her nobility she exalts herself over me.' So he said to him, 'Keep your wife to yourself.'" ﴿And fear Allah﴾ regarding her matter, so do not divorce her out of harm and as a pretext because of her haughtiness.

﴿And you concealed within yourself what Allah was to disclose﴾ which is his marrying her if he divorced her, or his intention to divorce her. ﴿And you feared the people﴾ their reproach of you because of it. ﴿And Allah has more right that you fear Him﴾ if there was in it what is to be feared. The *waw* is for the circumstantial state (*li'l-hal*). The reproach was not for concealment alone, since that is good, but for concealing it out of fear of people's talk and for displaying what contradicts what is hidden within, for in such matters it is better to remain silent or to entrust the matter to one's Lord. ﴿So when Zayd had accomplished his purpose from her﴾ meaning his need of her, to the extent that he became weary of her, no longer had any need of her, and divorced her, and her waiting period (*'idda*) ended. ﴿We married her to you﴾. It was also said that "accomplishing the purpose" is a metaphor for divorce, like "I have no need of you." It was read as "We married her to you" (*zawwajtukaha*), and the meaning is that He commanded her marriage to him, or made her his wife without an intermediary contract. This is supported by the fact that she used to say to the other wives of the Prophet, upon whom be blessings and peace: "Allah, the Exalted, arranged my marriage, while your guardians married you off." It was also said that Zayd was the envoy in her proposal, and that was a great trial and clear evidence of the strength of his faith. ﴿So that there may be no difficulty for the believers concerning the wives of their adopted sons when they have accomplished their purpose from them﴾ this is a reason (*'illah*) for the marriage, and it is evidence that his ruling and the ruling of the community are the same, except what the evidence specifies for him. And the command of Allah was His command, which He wills, a thing done (*maf'ulan mukawwanan*) without doubt, just as the marriage of Zaynab was.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 33, verses 38–39:

﴿There is no blame upon the Prophet in what Allah has ordained for him﴾. (It is) a portion allotted to him, and a usage of the expression "faraḍa lahu" (He allotted for him) in the register (al-dīwān); from it comes furūḍ al-ʿaskar (the army's allotments) for their provisions. ﴿The way of Allah﴾: He instituted this as a practice (sunnah). ﴿With those who passed away before﴾: among the prophets, and it is a negation of blame from them concerning what He permitted them. ﴿And the command of Allah is a decree decreed, a judgment finally settled﴾: a determined decree and a firmly fixed ruling.

﴿Who convey the messages of Allah﴾: an attributive clause for "those who passed away", or a praise (madḥ) in the accusative or nominative. It has also been read as "risālata Allāh" (the message of Allah, singular).

﴿And they fear Him and fear none but Allah﴾: an allusion after an explicit statement. ﴿And Allah suffices as a reckoner﴾: sufficient against fears, or one who calls to account, so that none should be feared except Him.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 33, verse 40:

﴿Muhammad is not the father of any one of your men﴾ in actual fact, so that between him and them there would be established what is established between a father and his son of prohibition by marriage (ḥurmat al-muṣāharah) and other things. Its generality is not undermined by his being the father of al-Ṭāhir, al-Qāsim and Ibrahim, because they did not reach the stage of men; and even had they reached it, they would have been his men, not your men. ﴿But he is the Messenger of Allah﴾, and every messenger is the father of his community, not in an absolute sense but in the sense that he is compassionate and sincerely advising towards them, and it is obligatory for them to revere and obey him. Zayd was among them, and there was no childbirth (wilādah) between him and the Prophet. It has been read as "Rasūlu Allāh" with the nominative (al-raf') on the basis that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, and "lakin" with the shaddah (tashdīd) on the basis of an omitted predicate, i.e., "but Messenger of Allah is whoever you know did not have a surviving male child."

﴿And the Seal of the Prophets﴾ and the last of them, the one who sealed them or by whom they were sealed according to the reading of ʿĀṣim with the fatḥah (al-fatḥ). Had he had an adult son, it would have been fitting for his rank that he be a prophet, as the Prophet ﷺ said concerning Ibrahim when he died: "If he had lived, he would have been a prophet." The descent of ʿĪsā after him does not detract from this, because when he descends he will be upon his religion; moreover, what is meant is that he is the last one to be sent as a prophet. ﴿And Allah is ever Knowing of all things﴾, so He knows who is fit to be the one with whom prophethood is sealed and how his affair should be conducted.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 33, verses 41–42:**

﴿O you who have believed, remember Allah with much remembrance﴾ — it encompasses all times and includes all kinds [of remembrance], with what is befitting of Him of sanctification (taqdis), praise (tahmid), declaration of His oneness (tahlil), and glorification (tamjid).

﴿And exalt Him morning and evening﴾ — specifically at the beginning of the day and at its end. Their being singled out for mention indicates their excellence over the rest of the times, since they are witnessed (by the angels), like the individual forms of glorification (tasbih) within the body of remembrances, because it is the foundation of them. It has been said that both verbs are directed toward these two times. It has also been said that what is meant by tasbih is the prayer (salah).

He it is who sends blessings upon you, [i.e., shows mercy to you], ﴿He it is who sends blessings upon you﴾ with mercy. ﴿And His angels﴾ [do so] by seeking forgiveness for you and by concern for what sets your affairs right. The meaning of "blessing" (ṣalāh) here is the common meaning, namely, care for the betterment of your affairs and the manifestation of your nobility, borrowed from ṣalw (the linguistic root meaning "bending" or "inclination"). It has also been said that compassion and spiritual inclination (al-inʿiṭāf al-maʿnawī) derive from ṣalāh, which involves the outward inclination that is bowing (rukūʿ) and prostration (sujūd). The angels' seeking forgiveness and their supplication for the believers is a form of compassion toward them, especially since it is a cause of mercy, inasmuch as they are those whose supplications are answered. ﴿To bring you out from darkness into light﴾: from the darknesses of disbelief and disobedience into the two lights of faith and obedience. ﴿And He is ever merciful to the believers﴾, in that He cared for the betterment of their affairs, elevated their station, and employed His honoured angels in this.

﴿Their greeting﴾ is an idafah of the verbal noun to its object, i.e., they will be greeted. ﴿On the day they meet Him﴾: the day of their meeting Him at death, or at their emergence from the graves, or at their entry into Paradise. ﴿Peace﴾: a report of safety from every disliked thing and calamity. ﴿And He has prepared for them a noble reward﴾: it is Paradise. Perhaps the variation in wording is for the sake of preserving the rhyme (fawāṣil) and for emphasis on what is more important.

O Prophet, indeed We have sent you as a witness (شاهدًا) over those to whom you were sent, over their affirmation and their denial, their salvation and their misguidance; and this is a circumstantial clause (حالٌ مُقَدَّرَةٌ), one whose condition is yet to come about. ﴿And a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾.

﴿And as one who calls to Allah﴾, to acknowledging Him, to His oneness, and to what belief in Him requires regarding His attributes. ﴿By His permission﴾, by His facilitating it. He stated it in absolute terms insofar as it is one of the means (of the call), and He restricted the call by it, as a notice that it is a difficult matter that cannot be accomplished except with help from His sacred presence. ﴿And as a radiant lamp﴾, by which one is illuminated away from the darkness of ignorance, and from whose light the lights of insight are kindled.

Give good tidings to the believers that they will have from Allah a great bounty (﴿وَبَشِّرِ المُؤْمِنِينَ بِأنَّ لَهم مِنَ اللَّهِ فَضْلا كَبِيرًا﴾), above all other nations, or in return for their deeds. It may be conjoined (ma'tuf) to something omitted, such as "so watch over the affairs of your community."

Do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites (﴿وَلا تُطِعِ الكافِرِينَ والمُنافِقِينَ﴾). This is an incitement for him against what they are upon, namely their opposition. And disregard their harm (﴿وَدَعْ أذاهُمْ﴾): their harming of you, and do not concern yourself with it; or your harming of them, as retribution or punishment for their disbelief. For this reason it was said that the verse is abrogated (mansukh, meaning superseded by a later ruling, naskh). And rely upon Allah (﴿وَتَوَكَّلْ عَلى اللَّهِ﴾), for He will suffice you against them. And Allah is sufficient as a Trustee (﴿وَكَفى بِاللَّهِ وكِيلا﴾): one to whom affairs are entrusted in all circumstances.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 33, verse 49:

﴿O you who have believed, when you marry believing women and then divorce them before you have touched them﴾ — i.e., before you have had intercourse with them. Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read it with an alif and a damma on the tā' (ṭallaqtumūhunna, i.e., "you have divorced them" in the form of "you have set them free"; the reading is "tamassūhunna" from the verb with the alif, i.e., "before you have touched them" in the sense of intercourse). ﴿Then you have no waiting period for them to count﴾ — days during which they wait, keeping themselves [from remarriage]. ﴿That you should count it⁠﴾ — you complete its number, from "ʿaddadtu al-darāhim" (I counted the dirhams) so that "iʿtaddahā" (he counted it), like your saying "kiltuhu fa-iktālahu" (I measured it for him and he measured it); or it means "tuʿiddūnahā" (you prepare it). The attribution to the men indicates that the waiting period is the right of the husbands, as the phrase ﴿So you have no [right]⁠﴾ implies. It is related from Ibn Kathīr that he read ﴿taʿtaddūnahā⁠﴾ with a single dāl, either by replacing one of the two dāls with a yā' or because it is from iʿtidāʾ, meaning "you transgress in it." Its apparent meaning requires that the waiting period is not obligatory merely by seclusion (khalwah). The specification of "believing women" while the ruling is general serves as a reminder that it is the nature of a believer not to marry except a believing woman, choosing for his seed. The function of "thumma" (then) is to remove what might be suspected: that the divorce is delayed for as long as the consummation could take place. Just as it affects lineage, it affects the waiting period. ﴿So provide for them⁠﴾ — that is, if no dowry was specified for them, for the one for whom a dowry was specified, the obligation is half of the specified dowry, not the provision (mut'ah). It is permissible to interpret "tamtīʿ" (providing) as covering both, or the command as shared between obligation and recommendation, since the provision is a sunnah for the one for whom a dowry was specified. ﴿And release them⁠﴾ — send them out of your homes, since you have no waiting period over them. ﴿A fair release⁠﴾ — without harm and without withholding of any right. It is not permissible to interpret it as the sunnah divorce, because that is arranged upon divorce, and the pronoun refers to those not yet consummated with.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 33, verse 50:

﴿O Prophet, indeed We have made lawful for you your wives to whom you have given their wages (ujur)﴾, meaning their dowries (mahr), because the mahr (the bridal gift) is a compensation (ajr) for the enjoyment of intimacy (al-bud'). The restriction of the lawfulness to giving the dowry promptly does not mean that lawfulness depends on it, but rather it is to prefer what is more excellent for him. It is like the restriction on the lawfulness of the slave woman by her being a captive (masbiyyah), in His words: ﴿and what your right hand possesses of what God has granted you as spoils﴾, since a purchased woman's situation and what has happened to her cannot be fully known at the outset. The restriction of the close relatives by their being emigrants with him, in His words: ﴿and the daughters of your paternal uncles, and the daughters of your paternal aunts, and the daughters of your maternal uncles, and the daughters of your maternal aunts, who emigrated with you﴾, is possible, and the restriction of lawfulness by that may be specific to him. This is supported by the statement of Umm Hani bint Abi Talib: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) proposed to me, and I excused myself to him, and he excused me. Then God revealed this verse, so I was not lawful to him, because I had not emigrated with him; I was among the al-Tulaqa' (those freed at the conquest of Makkah)."

﴿and a believing woman, if she gives herself to the Prophet﴾: it is in the accusative, governed by a verb that is explained by what precedes it, or it is coordinated with what came before. The restriction by the conditional particle "in" (if), which refers to the future, does not preclude this, since the meaning of the lawfulness is the informing of the lawfulness, that is: "We have informed you of the lawfulness of a believing woman who gives herself to you and does not demand a dowry, if it occurs." For this reason it is indefinite (nakkaraha). Scholars differed regarding whether this occurred and who it was. It is said there were four: Maymunah bint al-Harith, Zaynab bint Khuzaymah al-Ansariyyah, Umm Sharik bint Jabir, and Khawlah bint Hakim. It was also read with "an" (that) in the fatha form, meaning "because she gave herself," or "for the duration that she gives herself," like your saying: "Sit as long as Zayd is sitting."

﴿if the Prophet wishes to take her in marriage﴾: this is a condition for the first condition regarding the obligation of the lawfulness. Her giving herself to him does not make her lawful to him except by his wish to marry her, since it functions as the offer, and the shift from direct address to the third person by the repeated term "the Prophet" is intentional. Then the return to address him in His words: ﴿exclusively for you, apart from the believers﴾ is a notice that this is among what was specially granted to him because of the nobility of his prophethood, and an affirmation of his entitlement to this honor on his account. Our companions (the Shafi'i scholars) cited this as evidence that marriage is not concluded with the wording of gift (hibah), because the wording follows the meaning, and he (ﷺ) was specified with the meaning, so it is specified with the wording. Al-istinkah means seeking marriage and desiring it. "Khalisatan" (exclusively) is an emphatic infinitive, meaning that its lawfulness is purified, or that the lawfulness of what We have made lawful for you under the stated conditions is purified for you. Or it is a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun in "wahabat" (she gave), or an adjective of a deleted infinitive, meaning "a purified gift."

﴿We know what We have imposed upon them concerning their wives﴾: from the conditions of the contract, the obligation of equal division (qasm), and the dowry due by consummation when none was named. ﴿and what their right hands possess﴾: the widening of the matter regarding them, namely how it should be imposed on them. The clause is a parenthetical insertion between His words ﴿so that there may be no hardship upon you﴾ and its dependent element, which is "exclusively," to indicate that the distinction between him and the believers in such matters is not for the mere intention of widening things for him, but for purposes that require widening for him and restriction upon them at times, and the reverse at other times.

﴿And God is ever Forgiving﴾ of what is difficult to guard against, ﴿Merciful﴾ in extending latitude where hardship is likely.

﴿You may postpone whom you will of them﴾: you delay her and leave off lying with her. ﴿And you may take to you whom you will﴾: you draw her to you and lie with her. Or you may divorce whom you will and keep whom you will. Nafi', Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read ﴿turji﴾ with a yaa' (ﻱ), and the meaning is the same. ﴿And whomever you seek﴾: whomever you desire. ﴿of those you have set aside﴾: whom you have divorced with the option of return (raj'ah, the right to take her back during the waiting period). ﴿there is no blame upon you﴾ in any of that.

﴿That is more suitable that their eyes may be comforted and they will not grieve and will be pleased with what you give them, all of them﴾: that leaving the choice to your will is closer to comforting their eyes, to lessening their grief, and to their being pleased altogether, because the ruling concerning all of them is the same. Then, if you treat them equally, they will regard it as a favour from you, and if you prefer some of them, they will know that it is by the judgement of God, the Exalted, so their souls will be at rest with it. It is also recited as ﴿tuqirra﴾ with a damma on the taa' (تُقِرَّ), ﴿a'yunahunna﴾ with a fatha (أَعْيُنَهُنَّ) as the object, and ﴿tuqarru﴾ in the passive form (تُقَرُّ). ﴿kulluhunna﴾ is a corroborative (ta'kid) of the nun in ﴿yarda'na﴾ (يَرْضَيْنَ), and it is also recited in the accusative as a corroboration of ﴿hunna﴾. ﴿And God knows what is in your hearts﴾: so strive to do good in regard to it. ﴿And God is ever Knowing﴾ of what is within the breasts, ﴿Forbearing﴾, who does not hasten punishment, so He is deserving of being feared.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 33, verse 52:

﴿It is not lawful for you to take women﴾ with the ya' (in the verb yahillu), because the feminine marking of a plural noun is not real (ghayr haqiqi); and al-Basriyyan (the two Basran readers) read it with the ta' (tuhillu). ﴿after this﴾ i.e. after the nine; for him (the Prophet) this is like the four for us. Or: after today, so that if one of them dies, it is not lawful for him to marry another in her place. ﴿nor that you exchange them for other wives﴾ by divorcing one and marrying another in her place; and min (in min azwaj) is extra (mazidah), for emphasis of comprehensiveness (li-ta'kid al-istighraq). ﴿Even though their beauty pleases you﴾: the beauty of the wives who would be substituted. It is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the doer of tabaddala (the subject), not to its object, which is min azwaj, because of its extreme indefiniteness; its implied sense is: "your admiration for them being assumed." There is disagreement over whether the verse is muhkamah (unabrogated) or mansukhah (abrogated) by His saying: ﴿You may defer whom you will of them and take to you whom you will﴾ according to the second meaning, for although it precedes it in recitation, it comes after it in revelation (nuzul). It has also been said that the meaning is: "It is not lawful for you to take women after the four kinds of women whom He has explicitly made lawful for you, nor to exchange them for wives of other kinds."

﴿Except what your right hand possesses﴾: an exception from "women," since it includes both wives and slave-women; it has also been said to be a disjunctive exception (munqati'). ﴿And Allah is ever Watchful over all things﴾: so guard your affairs and do not transgress what has been set as limits for you.

(p-237)

﴿O you who believe, do not enter the houses of the Prophet unless you are given permission﴾, meaning: except at the time when permission is given to you, or except when you are permitted.

﴿for a meal﴾ is related to (yu'dhana, "is given permission"), because it implies the meaning of (yud'ā, "is invited"). This indicates that it is not proper to enter upon a meal without an invitation, even if permission is given, as His saying indicates: ﴿not waiting for its preparation﴾, meaning not waiting for its time or for it to be ready. It is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative, a term for a clause describing the state of the subject at the time of the action) from the subject of (do not enter), or from the pronoun in (lakum, "for you"). It was also read with the genitive (jarr) as an adjective (ṣifah) of (ṭaʿām, "meal"). In that case it follows a noun other than the one it refers to without an explicit pronoun, which the Basran grammarians (al-Baṣriyyūn, the grammarians of Basra) consider impermissible. Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī pronounced (ināhu) with imālah (vowel inclination), since it is a verbal noun from (anā al-ṭaʿām, "the meal ripened"), meaning when it was ready.

﴿But when you are invited, then enter; and when you have eaten, then disperse﴾, meaning scatter and do not linger. This address is to people who used to watch for the meal of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), entering and sitting while waiting for it to be ready. The ruling is specific to them and to those like them; otherwise it would not be permissible for anyone to enter his house with permission for something other than a meal, nor to remain after the meal for an important matter.

﴿Nor those who seek familiar conversation for discourse﴾, meaning engaging in talk with one another, or listening to the conversation of the household. It is conjoined with (nāẓirīna, "waiting for") or is governed by an implied verb, i.e., "do not enter, or do not remain, seeking familiar conversation."

﴿Indeed that [staying] was troubling the Prophet﴾, because of the narrowing of the dwelling upon him and his household, and his being occupied with what does not concern him. ﴿So he would be shy of you﴾, of having you leave, ﴿but Allah is not shy of the truth﴾. This means that your leaving is a truth, so it should not be neglected out of shyness, just as Allah does not abandon it through the abandonment of one who is shy; so He commanded you to leave. It was also read as (lā yastaḥī), with the first yāʾ dropped and its vowel transferred to the ḥāʾ.

﴿And when you ask them for a provision﴾, meaning something by which one benefits, ﴿then ask them from behind a screen﴾, meaning a partition.

It is narrated that ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "O Messenger of Allah, the righteous and the wicked enter upon you. Would that you commanded the Mothers of the Believers to veil themselves." So this verse was revealed.

It was also said that he (peace be upon him) was eating with some of his companions, and the hand of a man touched the hand of ʿĀʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her). The Prophet (ﷺ) disliked that, so this verse was revealed.

﴿That is purer for your hearts and their hearts﴾, from the soul's whisperings that come from Satan. ﴿And it is not for you﴾, meaning it is not proper for you, ﴿to harm the Messenger of Allah﴾, meaning to do what he dislikes. ﴿Nor to marry his wives after him, ever﴾, after his death or his separation from them. He specified the one he had not consummated with, because it was narrated that Ashʿath ibn Qays married the woman who sought refuge (al-mustaʿīdhah) in the days of ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him), and he resolved to stone her. He was informed that the Prophet (peace be upon him) had separated from her before he had touched her, so he left her without objection.

﴿Indeed that﴾, meaning harming him and marrying his wives, ﴿is in the sight of Allah an enormity﴾, a great sin. In this there is Allah's glorification of His Messenger and an affirmation of his sanctity, alive and dead. For this reason He emphasized the warning concerning it, saying:

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 33, verses 54–55:

﴿If you disclose a thing﴾, such as their marriage (to the Prophet), ﴿on your tongues﴾. ﴿Or conceal it﴾ ﴿in your breasts﴾. ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing of all things﴾, so He knows that and will recompense you for it. In this generalization, together with the evidence for the intended meaning, there is additional awe-inspiring warning and emphasis in the threat.

﴿There is no blame upon them concerning their fathers, their sons, their brothers, the sons of their brothers, the sons of their sisters﴾. This is an exception for those from whom veiling is not obligatory.

It is narrated: "When the verse of the veil was revealed, the fathers, the sons and the relatives said: 'O Messenger of Allah, shall we also speak to them from behind a veil?' So the verse was revealed."

The reason the paternal uncle and maternal uncle are not mentioned is that they are in the position of parents; for this reason the paternal uncle is called a father in His words, ﴿the God of your fathers, Abraham and Ishmael and Isaac﴾. ﴿Indeed, Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾ — they take care to manifest his nobility and magnify his station. ﴿O you who have believed, send blessings upon him﴾ — you too, take care of this, for you are more deserving of it; and say, "O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad." ﴿And greet him with a [worthy] greeting﴾ — and say, "Peace be upon you, O Prophet." It was also said: and submit to his commands. The verse indicates the obligation of sending blessings and peace upon him in general. It was said that sending blessings is obligatory whenever he is mentioned, based on his saying (ﷺ): "May he be humbled into the dust, the man in whose presence I am mentioned and he does not send blessings upon me," and his saying: "Whoever I am mentioned in the presence of and does not send blessings upon me, he has entered the Fire, and Allah has removed him far away." Sending blessings upon others is permissible by way of following (them), but it is disliked (makruh) to do so independently, because in common usage it has become a distinctive mark of the mention of the Messenger (ﷺ). For this reason it was disliked to say "Muhammad, Mighty and Majestic (ʿazza wa-jall)," even though he is mighty and majestic.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 33, verses 57–58:

﴿Indeed, those who abuse Allah and His Messenger﴾ commit what They both abhor, of disbelief and acts of disobedience; or they abuse the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) by breaking his front tooth, by calling him a poet or a madman, and the like. The mention of Allah here is for the sake of exalting Him. Whoever permits the use of a single expression with two meanings interprets it with both meanings, by considering the two objects (of the verb). ﴿Allah has cursed them﴾, that is, He has removed them far from His mercy. ﴿In this world and the Hereafter, and He has prepared for them a humiliating punishment﴾, which humiliates them along with the pain.

﴿And those who abuse believing men and believing women without their having earned it﴾ without a crime that would deserve the abuse. ﴿Then they have borne a slander and a manifest sin﴾, clear and evident. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 33, verse 60:

﴿If the hypocrites do not desist﴾ from their hypocrisy. ﴿And those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ weakness of faith and little steadfastness upon it; or, debauchery, arising from their wavering in religion or their immorality. ﴿And those who spread rumours in al-Madinah﴾ they spread bad news about the expeditions (sara;ya) of the Muslims and the like, from their agitation (irjaf). Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 33, verse 63:

﴿The people ask you about the Hour﴾ — about the time of its establishment, mockingly, or out of obstinacy, or as a test. ﴿Say: Its knowledge is only with Allah﴾ — He has not disclosed it to any angel or any prophet. ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near﴾ — "shay'an qariban" (something near), or "takunu al-sa'atu 'an qarib" (the Hour will be soon). Its being in the accusative (nasb) is as an adverb of time (zarf). It is also permissible that the masculine form (al-tadhkir) is used because al-sa'a (the Hour) carries the meaning of "the day." In it there is a warning to those who seek to hasten it, and a silencing of those who raise obstinate objections.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 33, verse 69:

﴿O you who believe, do not be like those who abused Musa (Moses), but Allah cleared him of what they said.﴾ So He made manifest his innocence from their saying, meaning its content and substance. This is because Qarun (Korah) incited a woman to accuse him of seducing her, but Allah protected him, as has passed in *al-Qasas* (the surah of the Narratives). Or some people accused him of killing Harun (Aaron) when he went out with him to Mount al-Tur (Sinai) and Harun died there. The angels then carried him and passed by him until they saw him was not killed. It is also said that Allah revived him and he informed them of his innocence. Or they slandered him with a defect in his body, such as leprosy (*baras*) or hernia (*udra*), because of his extreme concealment out of modesty, and so Allah made them aware that he was innocent of it. ﴿And he was honourable (*wajihan*) in the sight of Allah﴾, meaning possessing nearness and standing. It has also been recited as *"wa-kana ʿabda Allah wajihan"* (and he was the servant of Allah, honourable), where *ʿabd* (servant) is read in place of *ʿind* (in the sight of), with the same sense of honour in the sight of his Lord.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 33, verse 72:

﴿Indeed, We offered the trust (al-amanah) to the heavens and the earth and the mountains, but they refused to bear it and were apprehensive of it, and man bore it.﴾ This is a confirmation of the earlier promise concerning the magnification of obedience. He called it a trust (amanah) because it must be discharged. The meaning is that, because of the greatness of its status, if it had been offered to these great bodies and they had been possessed of awareness and perception, they would have refused to bear it, ﴿and were apprehensive of it, and man bore it﴾ despite the weakness of his constitution and the frailty of his strength. Undoubtedly, the one who tends it and upholds its rights attained the good of both abodes. ﴿Indeed, he was ever wrongdoing﴾ in that he did not fulfil it and did not observe its right. ﴿Ignorant﴾ of the ultimate consequence of it; and this is a description of the species in terms of the majority. It has been said that what is meant by "the trust" (al-amanah) is obedience, which encompasses both the natural and the voluntary; by "offering it" is meant soliciting it, which encompasses demanding the act from the one who chooses and wishing it to proceed from another; by "bearing it" is meant betrayal in it and abstention from discharging it, and from this is the saying "the bearer of the trust" (hamil al-amanah) and "its carrier" (muhtamiluha) for one who does not discharge it, so that his responsibility is cleared; thus, refusing it is an act of what can be expected of them, and "wrongdoing" and "ignorance" mean betrayal and negligence. It has also been said that when God Most High created these great bodies, He placed in them understanding and said to them: "Indeed, I have prescribed an obligation, and I have created a Garden for whoever obeys Me therein, and a Fire for whoever disobeys Me." They said: "We are subjected to what You have created us for; we do not bear an obligation, nor do we seek reward or punishment." And when He created Adam, He offered him the like of this, and he bore it, and he was a wrongdoer to himself by bearing what burdens it, ignorant of the grimness of its consequence. Perhaps what is meant by "the trust" is reason or moral responsibility (taklif), and by "offering it to them" is considering it in relation to their readiness (isti'dad); by their "refusal" is the natural refusal, which is the lack of fitness and readiness; and by "man's bearing it" is his receptivity and readiness for it, and his being a wrongdoer and ignorant because of what has overcome him of the irascible (ghadabiyyah) and appetitive (shahwiyyah) forces. On this view it is fitting that it be the cause of the bearing upon him, for among the benefits of reason is that it governs the two forces, guarding them against transgression and overstepping the bound; and the greater part of the intent of moral responsibility is to balance them and break their violence.

﴿That Allah may punish the hypocrite men and the hypocrite women, and the polytheist men and the polytheist women, and that Allah may turn in forgiveness to the believing men and the believing women﴾. This is a causal explanation (ta'lil) for the bearing (of the trust), inasmuch as it is its result, like discipline in the act of striking, which is a form of discipline. The mention of repentance in the promise indicates that their being wrongdoing and ignorant is part of their innate nature, which does not leave them free of lapses. ﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾, in that He repents of their lapses and rewards with success for their obedience.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Surah al-Ahzab and teaches it to his family or to those his right hand possesses, will be granted security from the punishment of the grave."
